sections.title: The prompt security threat landscape
sections.description: Prompt injection, jailbreaking, system prompt extraction, data exfiltration, and credential harvesting.

content.text: Prompt injection — malicious instructions embedded in user input or retrieved external content that override the system prompt or redirect the model's behavior beyond intended scope. Jailbreaking — user techniques for bypassing content policies and safety guardrails by framing requests in ways that circumvent trained refusals. System prompt extraction — users attempting to reveal the contents of the system prompt containing proprietary instructions, competitive intelligence, or configuration details. Data exfiltration — techniques for extracting training data, user data from other sessions, or sensitive information the model was given access to. Credential harvesting — social engineering the model into revealing API keys, connection strings, or other credentials included in its context.

items: Prompt injection — malicious instructions overriding system behavior.
Jailbreaking — bypassing content policies and safety guardrails.
System prompt extraction — revealing proprietary instructions.
Data exfiltration — extracting sensitive data from sessions.
Credential harvesting — extracting API keys and credentials.

sections.title: How prompt security differs from traditional application security
sections.description: Traditional security controls access through permissions; LLM security adds AI-specific layers for natural language threats.

content.text: Traditional application security controls access through authentication and authorization at the system level — you control what users can do through permission systems. LLM applications give users natural language flexibility that makes this boundary-drawing harder: the same input interface that enables legitimate creative queries also enables malicious manipulation. Prompt security adds AI-specific defensive layers — input validation for injection patterns, output monitoring for policy violations and data exfiltration signals, and runtime monitoring for anomalous interaction patterns — alongside traditional application security controls.

items: Traditional security — authentication, authorization, permissions.
AI-specific challenge — natural language flexibility blurs boundaries.
Input validation — detect injection patterns.
Output monitoring — policy violations and exfiltration signals.
Runtime monitoring — anomalous interaction patterns.

sections.title: Limitations and risks of prompt security

content.text: Prompt security has limitations. No single defense catches all injection variants. Sophisticated attackers can evolve beyond pattern detection. Output monitoring may generate false positives. LLM providers' safety training changes over time. Internal applications still face insider threats. Security controls can impact legitimate user experience. Red team testing is point-in-time and requires ongoing updates. Natural language flexibility makes perfect security unattainable.

items: No perfect defense — evolving injection variants.

Provider changes — safety training evolves over time.
Insider threats — internal applications still at risk.
User experience impact — security controls may affect UX.
Point-in-time testing — red teaming requires ongoing updates.
Unattainable perfection — natural language flexibility poses challenges.

faqs.title: Frequently asked questions about prompt security

items.question: Is prompt injection the same as SQL injection?
items.answer: Analogous in concept (injecting malicious instructions through an input interface) but different in mechanism — SQL injection exploits structured query parsing; prompt injection exploits the model's language understanding to override intended behavior.

items.question: Can input filtering prevent all prompt injection attacks?
items.answer: Filtering known patterns helps but isn't complete protection — sophisticated injection often evades pattern-matching; ClickMasters combines filtering with output monitoring and rate limiting for defense in depth.

items.question: What's the risk of a user extracting our system prompt?
items.answer: System prompt extraction reveals proprietary instructions and configuration — ClickMasters designs system prompts with extraction resistance and builds monitoring that alerts when extraction attempts occur.

items.question: Does prompt security need to be rebuilt for each LLM provider update?
items.answer: Application-level security controls are largely provider-agnostic and don't require rebuild for provider model updates — though new model capabilities sometimes require reassessment of the threat model.

items.question: How long does a prompt security assessment take?
items.answer: 6–20 weeks depending on application complexity and whether red team testing is included.

items.question: Is prompt security relevant for internal-only LLM applications?
items.answer: Yes — insider threat and accidental misuse risks apply to internal applications; the threat model differs from public-facing applications but prompt security remains relevant.

items.question: What is the difference between prompt injection and jailbreaking?
items.answer: Prompt injection overrides system instructions to change behavior; jailbreaking bypasses safety guardrails to enable prohibited content. Both are prompt security threats but target different types of restrictions.

items.question: Can prompt security protect against data exfiltration?
items.answer: Yes — output monitoring can detect patterns consistent with data exfiltration attempts, blocking or flagging responses that contain sensitive data before they reach the user.

items.question: How does prompt security handle multilingual attacks?
items.answer: Prompt security controls should be language-agnostic — ClickMasters designs detection and monitoring that works across languages, not just English-language injection patterns.
